title: The first sight: an old man
hook: on a chariot ride with Channa he sees a man bent with age and asks, will this happen to me
carry: this is coming for all of us
tomorrow: the second sight: a sick man

segments.voice: Yesterday: Yasodhara, she who bears glory, the prince's partner and later a nun in her own right. Your line: partner, not prize. Today, the road out of the palace.

A road swept clean and hung with decorations. And at the side of it, a man who was never supposed to be there. The stories say the young prince grew up without a single old face. His father, remembering the prophecy that his son might leave and become a teacher, kept every sad thing out of sight: three palaces, music, gardens, young and beautiful people everywhere. Then one day the prince asks his charioteer, Channa, to drive him out to the park. This is the first of four things he was never meant to see.
screen: `A ROAD SWEPT CLEAN.` → `A PALACE WITH NO OLD FACES.` → `A MAN BY THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: The man is bent almost double. Gray hair, few teeth, leaning on a stick, trembling as he walks. The prince has never seen anything like him. What's wrong with that man, the prince asks. His hair isn't like other people's. His body isn't like other bodies. Channa answers plainly: that's what we call an old man. Then the question the story turns on. Will this happen to me? Channa doesn't soften it. Yes. To you, to me, to everyone. Nobody gets past old age. The prince has the chariot turned around. No park today. He goes home and sits alone with it. One wrinkle in the sources: the Pali discourses tell the four sights about Vipassi, a Buddha of long ago. Later biographies tell it of Siddhattha, and that's the version in temples and picture books today. It echoes the Buddha's own quieter memory from the palaces: the pride of youth falling away. Either way, the point holds. The prince didn't learn a new fact; everyone knows people grow old. What changed is that he let it mean him. Old age stopped being something that happens to other people. That shift, from them to me, is where Buddhists say the path begins to open.
screen: `WHAT IS WRONG WITH THAT MAN?` · `WILL THIS HAPPEN TO ME?` · `A STORY TOLD OF AN OLDER BUDDHA.` · `FROM THEM TO ME.` · then, large: `THIS IS COMING FOR ALL OF US.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes, and bring to mind one old face you know well: the lines around the eyes, the hands. Let a quiet thought arrive: this face was once young like mine, and mine is on its way to this. Hold the two faces side by side, kindly, and let any gratitude come.
Channa. The prince's charioteer, who drove him past an old man and couldn't soften the truth. The first of four sights that turned his life around.
Your line: this is coming for all of us. Not a threat: just the plain answer Channa gave. That's day thirty-one.

howItsDone: Buddhists retell the four sights as the beginning of the Buddha's search, and one's own aging is the first of the five remembrances, which the Buddha said should be reflected on often.

fork.setup: you're the prince. your charioteer has just told you that you, too, will grow old. what do you do?

original.note: Pali: old age, aging. The first of the sights, and the first of the five remembrances.

trapdoor: what you thought: the prince had never seen an old person, which seems impossible.
what it means: the story is about the moment old age stops being about other people and starts being about you.
what a scholar hears: the four sights appear in the Mahapadana Sutta (DN 14) about the past Buddha Vipassi; the commentaries and later biographies transfer the story to Siddhattha.

chat.says: Everyone knows people get old. Why did seeing one old man change the prince?
options: He realized old age would happen to him too, not just to others.
The old man warned him that his father was hiding things.
He was scared because the old man looked sick and dangerous.
chat.meaning: Channa told him nobody gets past old age. The shift was from them to me: it would come for him too.

Channa.meaning: the prince's charioteer, who answered him plainly

Vipassi.meaning: a Buddha of long ago in the Pali discourses

Pali.meaning: the old language of the Theravada scriptures

sources.ref: Mahapadana Sutta (Digha Nikaya 14): the four sights, told of the Buddha Vipassi
Sukhumala Sutta (Anguttara Nikaya 3.38): the Buddha remembers the pride of youth falling away
Nidanakatha (introduction to the Jataka): the first sight on the road to the park

notes: The four sights: in the canon (DN 14) the story is told of Vipassi; the Nidanakatha and Buddhacarita tell it of Siddhattha. Confirm this framing is appropriate for the path.
In the Nidanakatha the gods place the old man on the road; that detail is left out here. A Keeper may want it in.
AN 3.38 paraphrased: the Buddha reflects that people are repelled by the old, forgetting they will age, and the intoxication of youth leaves him. Confirm wording.
Channa's answer that 'nobody gets past old age' follows DN 14's charioteer (all are subject to aging); confirm.
